extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in U.S. politics, media criticism, and recent political controversies
extracted.subtask_short: encyclopedic summary of Fake News Awards
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia article describing the creation, announcements, winners, and reception of Donald Trump's 'Fake News Awards', including the stated criteria and example stories cited as 'fake' or erroneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible for misrepresenting him and/or producing false reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Created to highlight the news outlets that he said were responsible for misrepresenting him and/or producing false reports both before, and during, his presidency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the lead: the awards were presented to outlets Trump said misrepresented him or published false reports. Examples given in the article include a range from social-media comments by journalists to news reports that later required corrections. The winners list (CNN, NYT, Washington Post, ABC, Newsweek, Time) and individual story notes illustrate this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonesty & bad reporting in various categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Awarding outlets for 'dishonesty & bad reporting in various categories' (phrase used by Trump in announcing the awards).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trump's January 2, 2018 tweet said he would award them for 'dishonesty & bad reporting in various categories.' The article documents that the 'awards' covered multiple types of alleged failures (fact errors, misleading posts, retractions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Most dishonest, corrupt and/or distorted in its political coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine which network/newspaper is 'the most dishonest, corrupt and/or distorted in its political coverage' (original tweet wording proposing the contest).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the November 27, 2017 tweet: 'We should have a contest as to which of the Networks... is the most dishonest, corrupt and/or distorted in its political coverage of your favorite President (me).' The Wikipedia article cites this as the initial framing for the awards/contest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ranking stories as 'fake', 'faker', or 'fakest' news
rubrics_metrics.description: Supporters were asked in an online poll to rank nominated stories as 'fake', 'faker', or 'fakest' news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trump's re‑election campaign sent emails linking to an online poll asking supporters to rank three nominated stories using the labels 'fake', 'faker', or 'fakest'. The article notes these poll labels as part of how winners were nominated/selected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reports that later required corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that contained factual errors and later required corrections or apologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple listed 'winners' were reports later corrected by the outlet (e.g., ABC's Brian Ross report on Michael Flynn, CNN's report on WikiLeaks access, Time's MLK bust tweet). The article notes corrections, apologies, temporary suspensions, and other remediations as evidence of error in reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bungled reports with significant real-world impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports containing major factual mistakes ('bungled report') that had measurable consequences (e.g., market movements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ABC News' Brian Ross bungled report on Michael Flynn, which ABC corrected and for which Ross was suspended; the erroneous report was linked to a temporary 350-point drop in the Dow Jones. The article treats such high-impact factual errors as qualifying for the awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erroneous reports later retracted and leading to staff consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports that were retracted and whose publication led to resignations or other staffing consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: CNN's report about Anthony Scaramucci's alleged ties to Russia was retracted; the story's fallout included resignations of three CNN staff members. The article highlights retractions and personnel consequences as markers of serious reporting failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misleading social-media posts (tweets/photos) that misrepresent events
rubrics_metrics.description: Tweets or social-media posts by journalists that misled about events (miscaptioned photos, deleted tweets, misleading claims) and required deletion or apology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Zeke Miller's tweet about a removed MLK bust (deleted after correction), Dave Weigel's misleading photo suggesting a small crowd, which was deleted and apologized for. The article lists such social-media errors among the awardees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Video or media presented out-of-context creating false impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Video or other media presented in a way that creates a false impression by omitting context (e.g., cropped clips implying careless or negative behavior).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: CNN published a video implying Trump carelessly overfed koi pond fish; the full video showed Trump copying Abe and the accompanying report actually portrayed Trump's actions positively. The article cites this as an instance of misleading presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short op-eds or opinion pieces with claims later changed or withdrawn
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinion pieces whose claims or predictions were later altered or retracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Paul Krugman's short op-ed predicting economic fallout was cited; Krugman changed the claim three days later. The article includes such pieces among the 'winners' to illustrate kinds of problematic commentary targeted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims of 'collusion' or major allegations that were unestablished
rubrics_metrics.description: High-profile claims (e.g., that the Trump campaign 'colluded' with Russia) that were publicly reported but not established by subsequent investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Wikipedia article notes an eleventh 'bonus' award went to reports about Russian interference and claims that the Trump campaign 'colluded' with Russia; the Special Counsel investigation was not finished at the time and ultimately 'never established that members of the Trump campaign conspired or coordinated with the Russian government.' The article treats publication of unestablished major allegations as a type of reporting failure targeted by the awards.
